evidence.claim: Route 41 crosses rural northwestern Connecticut in 17.86 miles, with a state border at each end.
evidence.quote: Route 41 is a 17.86-mile (28.74 km) scenic state highway in rural Northwestern Connecticut. It extends from the New York state line in Sharon to the Massachusetts state line in Salisbury

evidence.claim: The drive passes Mount Riga State Park, shares Main Street with US 44 between Salisbury and Lakeville, and runs through Sharon’s center.
evidence.quote: In Lakeville, Route 41 begins a 1.7-mile (2.7 km) overlap with U.S. Route 44 (Main Street), as the road heads into the town center of Salisbury.

evidence.claim: Connecticut’s scenic-road designation protects appearance by restricting changes including widening and rerouting.
evidence.quote: The scenic designation not only encourages sightseeing but also prevents certain developments alongside and on the road itself that would alter its appearance, including rerouting and widening.

evidence.claim: The modern road took shape in the 1932 highway renumbering, joining part of old New England Route 4 to State Highway 360.
evidence.quote: In the 1932 state highway renumbering, modern Route 41 was established from part of old New England Route 4 and old State Highway 360.

evidence.claim: Driving south from Massachusetts, follow Under Mountain Road past Mount Riga State Park to Salisbury center.
evidence.quote: In Salisbury center, Route 41 splits off from Route 44 along Under Mountain Road. The road travels for about 4.8 miles (7.7 km), passing by Mount Riga State Park, until the Massachusetts state line.

evidence.claim: The US 44 overlap leads to Lakeville; Sharon Road then passes the Route 112 junction south of Lake Wononscopomuc.
evidence.quote: Along the way, it intersects with Route 112 just south of Wononskopomuc Lake. In Lakeville, Route 41 begins a 1.7-mile (2.7 km) overlap with U.S. Route 44 (Main Street)

evidence.claim: Continue on Gay Street into Sharon, then through its Main Street center and onto Amenia Union Road for the New York line.
evidence.quote: Route 41 begins as Amenia Union Road at a junction with Dutchess County Route 2 in the hamlet of Amenia Union at the New York state line in the town of Sharon.

evidence.claim: Sharon’s long green is lined with Federal-period architecture, a legacy of the crossroads town’s early-19th-century prosperity.
evidence.quote: The town of Sharon was founded in 1739, and developed economically as a crossroads town, with its greatest period of economic prosperity in the early 19th century. This resulted in a preponderance of Federal period architecture lining the town's long green

evidence.claim: Railroads bypassed the village, but iron mines and furnaces supported its economy.
evidence.quote: Although the village was bypassed by railroads, it benefited economically in the 19th century from the presence of iron mines and furnaces.

evidence.claim: As those industries declined in the 1880s, tourism grew.
evidence.quote: By the 1880s, these industries were in decline, but the tourist trade was picking up.

evidence.claim: Country estates took over the southern part of the green, with new Colonial Revival houses and alterations to older buildings.
evidence.quote: The southern portion of the green was essentially taken over by large country estates, many either new Colonial Revival construction or significant alteration of older buildings.

evidence.claim: Four churches, the Romanesque library of 1893 and a memorial clock tower punctuate the civic center.
evidence.quote: Architecturally prominent are four church buildings, the 1893 Romanesque library, and the memorial clock tower located southeast of the main junction.

evidence.claim: In Sharon, residences and civic buildings line the long town green; farther north, the Undermountain Trail connects the highway to the Appalachian Trail.
evidence.quote: Centered around a mile-long town green are an array of public civic and religious buildings, as well as residences from the 18th to 20th centuries.

evidence.claim: the Undermountain Trail connects the highway to the Appalachian Trail.
evidence.quote: The Undermountain Trail connects to the northernmost section of the Appalachian Trail in Connecticut from the trail head at Mount Riga State Park's parking lot on Connecticut Route 41.

evidence.claim: The northern portion had briefly carried US 7 after its designation in 1926, before that highway moved to its modern alignment by 1928.
evidence.quote: In 1926, New England Route 4 was designated by AASHO as U.S. Route 7. By 1928, however, US 7 was relocated to its modern alignment.
